strengths: The paper addresses an important problem in visual multi-task learning: improving generalization alongside balancing task gradients. Separately aggregating loss and sharpness components is a concrete, modular idea compatible with several existing optimizers and requires no additional inference architecture.

The experiments cover classification, 40-attribute prediction, and dense scene understanding. Improvements recur across four gradient aggregation methods. For example, F-CAGrad improves MultiMNIST average accuracy from 95.01% to 95.95% and reduces CelebA average error from 8.52% to 8.22%.

Table 5 provides useful initial evidence for the proposed decomposition: on Cityscapes, separate aggregation improves segmentation mIoU from 68.93 to 73.77 over direct SAM-gradient aggregation, while also improving depth metrics.

The supplement strengthens the empirical analysis with calibration metrics, perturbation-radius sensitivity, training curves, and gradient-conflict measurements. Figure 1 and Algorithm 1 communicate the core procedure clearly, and the datasets, SAM/ASAM, and underlying aggregation methods are attributed.
weaknesses: The distinctive contribution is insufficiently isolated experimentally. The direct-versus-separate aggregation comparison appears only for MGDA on Cityscapes. Most other comparisons establish improvements over training without sharpness regularization. Comparisons with direct per-task ASAM across additional optimizers and datasets, and ASAM applied to a scalarized multi-task loss, are needed to establish the broader value of the proposed aggregation.

The theoretical motivation does not establish the claimed behavior of the algorithm. A componentwise interpretation of the vector maximum in Equation (4) does not imply a common worst-case shared perturbation. Moreover, Algorithm 1 perturbs shared and task-specific blocks separately, whereas the bound perturbs both jointly. Summing separately aggregated loss and flatness directions also need not produce descent for every task's robust objective. These connections require justification or more explicitly heuristic framing.

The formal guarantees need correction. In Appendix A, Theorem 3 allocates failure probability across events without updating the corresponding logarithmic penalties; a simultaneous taskwise guarantee requires accounting for this allocation. Theorem 4's Gaussian-tail correction also omits the loss-bound factor L. These appear repairable, but applicability of the bounded-loss and Gaussian-perturbation assumptions to the implemented objectives remains unestablished.

Reproducibility and computational practicality are incompletely documented. Appendix C reports using adaptive SAM, while Algorithm 1 specifies ordinary Euclidean SAM; the implemented adaptation and selected perturbation radii need clarification. Task-specific perturbed evaluations introduce additional training cost, but runtime, memory, and comparisons under equal computational budgets are absent, particularly relevant for CelebA's 40 tasks.

Aggregate improvements should not be presented as improvements on every task. On NYUv2, F-MGDA reduces segmentation mIoU from 30.47 to 26.42, and F-PCGrad worsens several surface-normal metrics. These tradeoffs deserve explicit analysis. Tables 2–4 also omit variability estimates, limiting conclusions about small differences such as CelebA errors of 8.22 versus 8.23.
